title: The Adjugate Behind Cramer's Rule and Cayley–Hamilton
description: The parent chain (cramers-rule) develops Cramer's rule via the adjugate. This entry answers its OQ-04-OQ-01: formalize the algebraic Cayley–Hamilton proof via the adjugate-reflexive identity adj(xI−A)·(xI−A) = χ_A(x)·I. Both Cramer's rule and Cayley–Hamilton rest on the same identity adj(B)·B = (det B)·I — Cramer applies it to a scalar matrix, Cayley–Hamilton to the characteristic matrix xI−A over R[X]. We package the adjugate identities, Cayley–Hamilton, minpoly ∣ charpoly, and the determinant form of Cramer's rule A·(adj A · b) = (det A)·b, with 0 axioms.

overview.historicalContext:
The adjugate (classical adjoint) of a square matrix A is the transpose of its cofactor matrix, and it satisfies the fundamental identity adj(A)·A = A·adj(A) = (det A)·I. This single identity underlies two cornerstones of linear algebra. **Cramer's rule** applies it to A itself: when det A is invertible, A⁻¹ = (det A)⁻¹·adj(A), so the system Ax = b has the explicit solution x = (det A)⁻¹·adj(A)·b. The **Cayley–Hamilton theorem** applies it to the characteristic matrix B = xI − A over the polynomial ring R[X]: since det(xI − A) = χ_A(x), the identity reads adj(xI − A)·(xI − A) = χ_A(x)·I, and passing to Polynomial (Matrix n n R) and evaluating at A telescopes the right factor to zero, yielding χ_A(A) = 0.

Mathlib formalizes the adjugate identity (adjugate_mul, mul_adjugate) and proves Cayley–Hamilton exactly via this route (aeval_self_charpoly, whose proof opens with adjugate (charmatrix M) * charmatrix M = M.charpoly • 1). This entry answers the parent's OQ-04-OQ-01 by exposing the adjugate-reflexive identity as a named lemma, restating Cayley–Hamilton and its minpoly consequence, and recording the determinant form of Cramer's rule — making explicit that both theorems flow from the same adjugate identity.
overview.problemStatement: Formalize the algebraic Cayley–Hamilton theorem via the adjugate-reflexive identity adj(xI − A)·(xI − A) = χ_A(x)·I, and tie it to Cramer's rule through their shared adjugate identity adj(B)·B = (det B)·I. Record Cayley–Hamilton, minpoly ∣ charpoly, and the determinant form of Cramer's rule.
overview.proofStrategy: adjugate_charmatrix_mul is adjugate_mul applied to the characteristic matrix charmatrix M, using that charpoly M is by definition det(charmatrix M). cayley_hamilton restates Mathlib's aeval_self_charpoly (proved by lifting the adjugate identity to Polynomial (Matrix n n R) and evaluating at A). minpoly_dvd_charpoly is Mathlib's lemma. adjugate_mulVec_solve rewrites A·(adj A · b) via mulVec associativity to (A·adj A)·b = (det A · I)·b = det A · b, using mul_adjugate, smul_mulVec_assoc, one_mulVec.
keyInsights: One identity, two theorems: adj(B)·B = (det B)·I gives Cramer's rule when B = A (scalar entries) and Cayley–Hamilton when B = xI − A (polynomial entries).

Cayley–Hamilton is NOT obtained by naively substituting x = A into χ_A(x)·I = adj(xI−A)·(xI−A): the coefficient ring Matrix n n R is non-commutative, so one must work in Polynomial (Matrix n n R) and evaluate, where the right factor (xI − A) telescopes to zero.
The determinant form of Cramer's rule A·(adj A · b) = (det A)·b is the adjugate identity applied to a vector; dividing by det A (when invertible) gives the classical explicit solution.
Over a field, Cayley–Hamilton immediately yields minpoly A ∣ charpoly A, bounding the degree of the minimal polynomial by n.
Exhibiting the shared adjugate source clarifies why determinants, inverses (Cramer), and the characteristic polynomial (Cayley–Hamilton) are facets of one cofactor identity.
